docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
Back to Model Calibration

An ObservedDataPoint says what the model must reproduce: an output at a position on the axis. This page shows how to observe several outputs, sums of outputs, partial observations (factors), counts per period (windows) and positions between integers, and how to weigh them.

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
from commol import (
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)

def model(k1: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Observed")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
        .add_accumulator(id="cum_ab", name="Total moved from A to B")
        .add_transition(
            id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total", accumulators=["cum_ab"]
        )
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .set_initial_conditions(
            total=1000,
            bin_fractions=[
                {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
                {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
                {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
            ],
        )
        .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
    )

truth = Simulation(model(0.4)).run(num_steps=70)

def calibrate_k1(observed_data, **problem_options) -> float:
    problem = CalibrationProblem(
        observed_data=observed_data,
        parameters=[
            CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0)
        ],
        optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
        **problem_options,
    )
    result = Calibrator(Simulation(model(None)), problem).run()
    return round(result.best_parameters["k1"], 3)

# Observe B and C at the same steps
observed = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output=output, value=truth[output][step])
    for step in range(10, 51, 10)
    for output in ("B", "C")
]
print(calibrate_k1(observed))  # 0.4

Each observation compares the model output named in output with value at the position at. Any output works: a compartment (B, B_g1) or an accumulator (cum_ab). The observation's label names its series in reports, plots and the per-series normalization; it defaults to output.

Field Type Default Meaning at float required The position on the axis. The engine decides which positions its model type accepts. output str \| None None The observed output. Give output or outputs, not both. outputs list[str] \| None None Outputs summed before the comparison; needs a label. label str output The name of the observed series. value float required The observed value, not negative. weight float 1.0 How much the observation counts in the loss. factor_id str \| None None A factor unknown that multiplies the prediction. window float \| None None Compares with the gain over (at − window, at] instead of the value.

An unknown field, such as a misspelt name, raises ValidationError and names it.

docs.title: Sums of outputs
docs.text:
When one measurement covers several outputs, list them in outputs. They are summed before the comparison; label names the sum for plots and reports:

b_and_c = [
    ObservedDataPoint(
        at=step,
        label="B_plus_C",
        outputs=["B", "C"],
        value=truth["B"][step] + truth["C"][step],
    )
    for step in range(10, 51, 10)
]
print(calibrate_k1(b_and_c))  # 0.4

outputs may name compartments and accumulators, and works with factor_id and window. It must not be empty.

docs.title: Weights and normalization
docs.text:
Option Where Effect weight=2.0 ObservedDataPoint The observation counts twice as much in every loss: its squared (or absolute) residual is multiplied by 2. See Losses. normalize_observations=True CalibrationProblem Divides each residual by the RMS of its series, so a series of thousands does not drown a series of tens. 
weighted = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=10, output="B", value=truth["B"][10], weight=2.0),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=30, output="B", value=truth["B"][30], weight=1.0),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=30, output="cum_ab", value=truth["cum_ab"][30], weight=1.0),
]
print(calibrate_k1(weighted, loss_function="sse", normalize_observations=True))  # 0.4

docs.title: Partial observations: factors
docs.text:
When the data sees only part of an output, for example a fixed share of it, a factor unknown multiplies the prediction before the comparison. Link observations to it with factor_id:

seen = 0.3
partial = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=seen * truth["B"][step], factor_id="share_seen")
    for step in range(5, 51, 5)
]

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=partial,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="share_seen", parameter_type="factor", min_bound=0.01, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
)
scaled_result = Calibrator(Simulation(model(0.4)), problem).run()
print(round(scaled_result.best_parameters["share_seen"], 3))  # 0.3
Fact Detail Several factors Each observation names its own factor_id, so outputs can have different shares. Not part of the model apply_calibration_parameters skips factor values. Plots Pass calibration_result= to SimulationPlotter.plot_series; it applies the calibrated factors to the comparison. Identifiability A rate and a share can explain the same data. Fit them together only when the data can tell them apart.

docs.title: Counts per period: windows
docs.text:
Data often counts what happened in each period, such as new arrivals per week. Observe a cumulative output (an accumulator) with window, and the model's prediction becomes the gain over the window:

predicted(at) = output(at) - output(at - window)

from commol import window_ends, windowed_totals

weekly_ends = window_ends(window=7, end=70)
weekly_counts = windowed_totals(truth["cum_ab"], truth.positions, 7, weekly_ends)

weekly = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=end, output="cum_ab", value=count, window=7)
    for end, count in zip(weekly_ends, weekly_counts)
]
print(calibrate_k1(weekly))  # 0.4
Rule Detail window <= at Otherwise the observation is rejected when it is created. Any output Usually an accumulator, but any compartment works. Mixed windows Observations may use different windows, and positions need not be multiples of the window. Combinations Works with factor_id and outputs.

windowed_totals (module function) and Simulation.windowed_totals apply the same reduction outside calibration, so a report shows exactly what the loss compared. See Windowed totals.

docs.title: Positions between integers
docs.text:
A DifferentialEquations model runs in continuous time, so an observation may be at any position, such as 2.5, and a window may cover any length. The calibration reads the engine at those positions (SimulationEngine::run_at_positions_into_buffer). The engine decides which positions its model type accepts (SimulationEngine::check_position): a DifferenceEquations model reports only at integer steps, so Calibrator raises ValueError for any other position, and the engine's message names the observation, or the constraint, that holds it (check_positions in crates/commol-calibration/src/calibration_problem.rs).

def ode_model(k1: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Observed in continuous time")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
        .set_initial_conditions(
            total=1000,
            bin_fractions=[{"bin": "A", "fraction": 1.0}, {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.0}],
        )
        .build(engine="DifferentialEquations")
    )

positions = [0.5, 1.75, 3.25, 6.5]
observed_b = Simulation(ode_model(0.2)).run_at(positions)["B"]
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        ObservedDataPoint(at=at, output="B", value=value)
        for at, value in zip(positions, observed_b)
    ],
    parameters=[CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0)],
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
)
print(round(Calibrator(Simulation(ode_model(None)), problem).run().best_parameters["k1"], 3))  # 0.2

docs.title: Stratified models
docs.text: Observe expanded outputs by name, such as B_g1, or sum them with outputs. Simulation.outputs_for("B") lists the names.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Every output (and every entry of outputs) is an output name; a sum has a label.
  • [ ] Weights say how much each observation counts, in every loss.
  • [ ] Every factor_id has a CalibrationParameter with parameter_type="factor".
  • [ ] Windowed observations use a cumulative output and window <= at.

docs.title: Optimizers
docs.text:
Back to Model Calibration

The class of optimization_config chooses the optimizer: NelderMeadConfig for a fast local search, ParticleSwarmConfig for a global one. Both run in Rust on the argmin library, and both keep every unknown inside its bounds.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text:
Optimizer Strength Weakness Use when Nelder-Mead Few evaluations; precise near the answer Local: can stop at a bound or a local minimum Few unknowns, a good initial_guess Particle swarm Searches the whole box; robust to local minima Many evaluations Several unknowns, no good starting point

A common pattern: run particle swarm first, then Nelder-Mead from its result with initial_guess.

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
from commol import (
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    ParticleSwarmConfig,
    Simulation,
)

def model(k1: float | None, k2: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Optimizers")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .set_initial_conditions(
            total=1000,
            bin_fractions=[
                {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
                {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
                {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
            ],
        )
        .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
    )

truth = Simulation(model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=50)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step])
    for step in range(5, 51, 5)
]

def calibrate(optimization_config) -> dict[str, float]:
    problem = CalibrationProblem(
        observed_data=observed_data,
        parameters=[
            CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
            CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
        ],
        optimization_config=optimization_config,
        seed=7,
    )
    result = Calibrator(Simulation(model(None, None)), problem).run()
    return {name: round(value, 2) for name, value in sorted(result.best_parameters.items())}

print(calibrate(NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000)))                    # {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}
print(calibrate(ParticleSwarmConfig(num_particles=30, max_iterations=300)))  # {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}

docs.title: Nelder-Mead
docs.text:
nelder_mead = NelderMeadConfig(
    max_iterations=1000,
    sd_tolerance=1e-6,
    initial_simplex_size=0.1,
    alpha=1.0,
    gamma=2.0,
    rho=0.5,
    sigma=0.5,
    verbose=False,
    header_interval=100,
)
print(calibrate(nelder_mead))  # {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}
Field Default Meaning max_iterations 1000 The iteration limit. sd_tolerance 1e-6 Stops when the spread of the simplex values falls below it. initial_simplex_size 0.1 The size of the first simplex: each vertex moves one unknown by this fraction of its bound width, towards the farther bound. In (0, 1]. alpha, gamma, rho, sigma None (argmin defaults) Reflection, expansion, contraction and shrink coefficients. verbose False Prints a progress table. header_interval 100 With verbose, repeats the table header every this many iterations.

The search starts at initial_guess, or at the midpoint of the bounds; a start of 0 works. Nelder-Mead searches an unbounded coordinate u and scores x = lo + (hi − lo)·(sin u + 1)/2 (the transform of MINUIT and lmfit), so every value it tries is inside the bounds (SineTransform in crates/commol-calibration/src/optimization.rs). An optimum exactly at a bound is reached only asymptotically, so it can take more iterations.

docs.title: converged and termination_reason
docs.text:
termination_reason converged Meaning Terminated(SolverConverged) True Nelder-Mead: the spread of the simplex values fell below sd_tolerance Terminated(TargetCostReached) True Particle swarm: the loss reached target_cost Terminated(MaxItersReached) False The run used all max_iterations Any other reason False The run stopped for another reason, such as a timeout

converged comes from converged in optimization.rs. A particle swarm without target_cost always stops at max_iterations, so it reports converged=False; judge it by final_loss.

docs.title: Particle swarm
docs.text:
swarm = (
    ParticleSwarmConfig(num_particles=40, max_iterations=300, initialization="latin_hypercube")
    .inertia("chaotic", w_min=0.4, w_max=0.9)
    .acceleration("time_varying", c1_initial=2.5, c1_final=0.5, c2_initial=0.5, c2_final=2.5)
    .velocity(clamp_factor=0.2, mutation_threshold=0.005)
    .mutation("gaussian", scale=0.1, probability=0.05, application="global_best")
)
print(calibrate(swarm))  # {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}
Field Default Meaning num_particles 20 The swarm size. More particles search more widely and cost more evaluations. max_iterations 1000 The iteration limit. initialization "uniform" Where particles start: "uniform", "latin_hypercube" (spread evenly) or "opposition_based" (each random point with its mirror). verbose False Prints progress.

Each method returns the configuration, so they chain:

Method Arguments Effect .inertia("constant", factor=0.721) factor A fixed inertia weight. .inertia("chaotic", w_min=…, w_max=…) w_min < w_max An inertia weight that varies chaotically between the two. .acceleration("constant", cognitive=1.193, social=1.193) cognitive, social Fixed pulls towards each particle's best and the swarm's best. .acceleration("time_varying", c1_initial=…, c1_final=…, c2_initial=…, c2_final=…) four factors Pulls that change from explore (high c1) to exploit (high c2). .velocity(clamp_factor=None, mutation_threshold=None) fractions clamp_factor limits speed to a share of the search box (0.1–0.2 is typical); mutation_threshold restarts particles slower than it (0.001–0.01). .mutation(strategy, *, scale, probability, application) see right Random jumps to escape local minima: strategy "gaussian" or "cauchy" (larger jumps), probability per iteration, application "global_best", "all_particles" or "below_average".

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Set CalibrationProblem(seed=...): particle swarm, the initialization and the probabilistic ensemble then make the same random choices on every run.

docs.title: History of evaluations
docs.text: Calibrator.run_with_history() returns the result and every evaluation the optimizer made, which is what probabilistic calibration builds its ensembles from.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Try A result sits at a bound Check the bounds, give a better initial_guess, or use particle swarm converged=False Check termination_reason: with MaxItersReached, raise max_iterations Different results on each run Set seed; use more particles or iterations A good loss but implausible values Unknowns that the data cannot tell apart; fix one, or add observations Slow Fewer observation steps or particles; Nelder-Mead from a good start

docs.title: Model Calibration
docs.text:
Back to Home

Calibration finds the parameter values (and, if you want, initial conditions and observation scale factors) that make a model reproduce observed data. You describe the observations and the unknowns in a CalibrationProblem, and a Calibrator runs an optimizer in the Rust engine.

Topic Page The workflow, the problem, losses and results This page Calibrating initial conditions Calibrating Initial Conditions Several outputs, aggregates, weights, scale factors, windowed data Observations Nelder-Mead and particle swarm settings Optimizers Relations the result must respect Constraints Reports of a calibrated model and run Reports Ensembles and confidence intervals Probabilistic Calibration

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
from commol import (
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)

def basic_model(k1: float | None, k2: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .set_initial_conditions(
            total=1000,
            bin_fractions=[
                {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
                {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
                {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
            ],
        )
        .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
    )

# Observations generated from k1 = 0.4, k2 = 0.1
truth = Simulation(basic_model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=50)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step])
    for step in range(5, 51, 5)
]

# 1. A model whose unknowns are None
model = basic_model(None, None)

# 2. The problem: observations, unknowns, loss and optimizer
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
    seed=42,
)

# 3. Calibrate
result = Calibrator(Simulation(model), problem).run()
print({name: round(value, 3) for name, value in sorted(result.best_parameters.items())})
# {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}

# 4. Write the values back, and simulate
model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)
calibrated = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)

A Simulation follows its model: after apply_calibration_parameters or update_parameters, its next run (and its engine) uses the new values, also when it was created while a parameter was None. See Simulations.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: CalibrationProblem field Type Default Meaning observed_data list[ObservedDataPoint] required What the model must reproduce. See Observations. parameters list[CalibrationParameter] required The unknowns and their bounds. loss_function str "sse" How the misfit is measured; see Losses. optimization_config NelderMeadConfig or ParticleSwarmConfig required The optimizer and its settings. See Optimizers. constraints list[CalibrationConstraint] [] Relations the result must respect. See Constraints. normalize_observations bool False Divides each residual by the RMS of its observation series, so series of very different size weigh the same. initial_condition_remainder str \| None None The compartment or bin that absorbs the difference when initial conditions are calibrated. See Calibrating Initial Conditions. probabilistic_config ProbabilisticCalibrationConfig \| None None Turns the problem into an ensemble calibration. See Probabilistic Calibration. seed int \| None None Makes every random choice reproducible.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text: ObservedDataPoint field Type Default Meaning at float required The position of the observation on the axis. A difference model accepts integer steps only. output str \| None None The output it observes: a compartment or accumulator name, such as B or B_g1. Give output or outputs. outputs list[str] \| None None Outputs to sum before the comparison; needs a label. label str output The name of the observed series in reports, plots and the normalization. value float required The observed value. weight float 1.0 How much the observation counts in every loss; see Losses. factor_id str \| None None A factor parameter that multiplies the prediction. window float \| None None Compares with the gain over (at − window, at] instead of the value.

docs.title: Unknowns
docs.text:
CalibrationParameter field Type Default Meaning id str required What to calibrate; depends on parameter_type. parameter_type str required "parameter", "initial_condition" or "factor". min_bound, max_bound float required The search interval. initial_guess float \| None None Where the optimizer starts; the midpoint of the bounds if None. parameter_type id names The value is "parameter" A model parameter, usually declared with value=None The parameter value "initial_condition" A bin, a category, or an expanded compartment A fraction of the total; see Calibrating Initial Conditions "factor" Any new id, used by observations through factor_id A factor on the predictions; not part of the model

"parameter" and "factor" work with every kind of model. The other types are values of the model kind, and the kind declares which it accepts (model.structure.calibration_value_types()): a compartmental model accepts "initial_condition". A type the kind does not accept raises a ValueError that names the kind when you create the Calibrator.

docs.title: Losses
docs.text:
loss_function Formula (residual r = observed − predicted, weight w) Use when "sse" (default) Σ w·r² The usual choice "rmse" √(Σ w·r² / Σ w) You want the error in the data's unit "mae" Σ w·|r| / Σ w The data has outliers

How weights count

Every loss uses a weight the same way: weight=2.0 makes an observation count twice as much as one with weight 1.0. With every weight at its default of 1.0, the losses are the plain sum of squares, root mean square and mean absolute error. LossConfig in crates/commol-calibration/src/types.rs computes them, for the optimizer and for the ensemble central loss.

With normalize_observations=True, each residual is first divided by the RMS of the observations of its series (its label).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Calibrator(simulation, problem) checks the problem against the model, and run() returns a CalibrationResult:

CalibrationResult field Meaning best_parameters dict[str, float]: the best value of every unknown final_loss The loss at best_parameters iterations The optimizer iterations performed converged True only when the optimizer met its convergence test or target_cost; a run that used all max_iterations is False. See Optimizers. termination_reason Why it stopped 
print(result.converged, result.termination_reason)
print(f"loss = {result.final_loss:.3g} after {result.iterations} iterations")
Calibrator member What it does run() Runs the optimizer and returns a CalibrationResult. run_with_history() Also returns every evaluation the optimizer made. run_probabilistic() Runs an ensemble calibration; needs probabilistic_config. num_observations, num_parameters, parameter_names Facts about the problem.

docs.title: Writing the result back
docs.text:
Model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem) writes every calibrated value into the model, routed by its parameter_type:

parameter_type Written to "parameter" The model parameter with that id "initial_condition" The initial conditions, so the model rebuilds exactly the state the optimizer scored "factor" Nothing: it describes the observations, not the model

It accepts a CalibrationResult, a ProbabilisticCalibrationResult (it then applies the ensemble's point_parameters) or a plain {id: value} mapping. It computes the new definition first, so a rejected value leaves the model unchanged. To set values by hand, use Model.update_parameters({...}).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Every unknown is None in the model and has a CalibrationParameter.
  • [ ] Every observation names an output of the model (Simulation.simulation_outputs).
  • [ ] The bounds are realistic, and the result is not stuck at a bound.
  • [ ] result.converged is True, or you know why not.
  • [ ] You simulate the calibrated model with a new Simulation.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Back to Home

A Commol model is a set of compartments that each hold an amount, and transitions that move amounts between them at each step. The amounts of every compartment together are the state of the model, and their sum is the total. An amount can be a count, a mass or a concentration. This page explains each building block once, with a runnable example. For every option of every method, see Building Models.

docs.title: The concepts at a glance
docs.text: Concept What it is Builder method Compartment (bin) A state that holds an amount add_bin Stratification A dimension that splits every compartment into categories add_stratification Parameter A named constant or formula used in rates add_parameter Transition A flow between compartments, with a rate add_transition Accumulator A counter of what a transition moved; not part of the state add_accumulator Initial conditions The total and how it is split at the start set_initial_conditions Model The validated definition build Simulation Runs a model for a number of steps Simulation(model).run

docs.title: Compartments
docs.text:
A compartment (a bin) holds an amount: a part of the total. A model can have any number of them, with any ids.

from commol import ModelBuilder, Simulation

builder = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Concepts")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A parameter is a named value that rates can use. Its value is a number, a formula (a string that can use other parameters and the special variables), or None when calibration will find it.

builder = (
    builder
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3, description="A to B rate")
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1, description="B to C rate")
)

docs.title: Transitions
docs.text:
A transition moves an amount from its source compartments to its target compartments at each step. How much it moves depends on its rate:

The rate… Kind Flow per step Example names a compartment, a bin total or total Absolute the rate itself "k1 * A * B / total" names no compartment Per-capita rate × source "k2" moves k2 × B 
builder = (
    builder
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
)

The engine decides the kind when the model is built, and model.print_equations() shows the result: the per-capita rate above prints as k2 * B. See Design decisions for the exact rule.

docs.title: Accumulators
docs.text:
An accumulator counts what a transition has moved since step 0. It is an output of the simulation, not part of the state: nothing is ever taken from it, and it is not part of the total.

builder = builder.add_accumulator(id="cum_ab", name="Total moved from A to B")
builder = builder.add_transition(
    id="t_ab_counted",
    source=["A"],
    target=["B"],
    rate="0.01 * A",
    accumulators=["cum_ab"],
)

With stratifications, an accumulator expands like a bin (cum_ab_g1, cum_ab_g2, …). Resetting a simulation sets it back to 0.

docs.title: Initial conditions
docs.text:
The initial conditions give the total and the fraction of it that starts in each bin. The total is a real number, finite and greater than 0:

builder = builder.set_initial_conditions(
    total=1000,
    bin_fractions=[
        {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.9},
        {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.1},
        {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
    ],
)
Rule Checked when total is finite and greater than 0 The conditions are set Each fraction is between 0.0 and 1.0 The conditions are set The bin fractions sum to 1.0 The conditions are set Every bin has a fraction The model is built Every stratification has fractions, and they sum to 1.0 The model is built

A fraction may be None when calibration will find it; see Model Calibration.

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
build validates the definition and returns a Model. Simulation runs it in the Rust engine:

model = builder.build(engine="DifferenceEquations")

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=50)

print(sorted(results))   # ['A', 'B', 'C', 'cum_ab']
print(len(results["A"]))  # 51: step 0 to step 50

A Model has a header (its name, parameters and step unit), the engine that runs it, and its structure: the part of its kind. ModelBuilder builds the compartmental kind, so model.structure is a CompartmentalStructure that holds the bins, stratifications, transitions and initial conditions:

print(model.engine.type)                    # DifferenceEquations
print(model.structure.kind)                 # compartmental
print([b.id for b in model.structure.bins])  # ['A', 'B', 'C']

Two engines run a compartmental model, with the same structure:

Engine Time Crate DifferenceEquations Advances in whole steps; each step applies every flow once. commol-difference DifferentialEquations Continuous: the engine integrates dX/dt = Σ flows with an ODE solver. commol-differential

See Differential equations.

docs.title: Stratifications
docs.text:
A stratification splits every compartment into one compartment per category. The expanded name is {bin}_{category}, with one suffix per stratification, in the order the stratifications are declared:

Bins: A, B           Stratification group = [g1, g2]

A -> A_g1, A_g2
B -> B_g1, B_g2      4 compartments (2 bins x 2 categories)

With several stratifications, the expansion is the product of all their categories:

Stratifications group = [g1, g2] and type = [t1, t2]

A -> A_g1_t1, A_g1_t2, A_g2_t1, A_g2_t2      8 compartments for 2 bins

The initial amount of each compartment is the total times the product of its fractions:

stratified = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Stratified")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=10000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.9},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.1},
        ],
        stratification_fractions=[
            {
                "stratification": "group",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "g1", "fraction": 0.6},
                    {"category": "g2", "fraction": 0.4},
                ],
            }
        ],
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

for compartment in stratified.structure.initial_state():
    print(compartment.name, compartment.amount)
Compartment Calculation Initial amount A_g1 10000 × 0.9 × 0.6 5400 A_g2 10000 × 0.9 × 0.4 3600 B_g1 10000 × 0.1 × 0.6 600 B_g2 10000 × 0.1 × 0.4 400

CompartmentalStructure.initial_state() returns this table as the engine builds it: each compartment with its bin, its categories and its amount.

Use a stratification when subgroups have different rates, when you need output per subgroup, or when the data you fit is broken down by category.

docs.title: Conditional stratifications
docs.text:
A stratification with conditions only splits the compartments whose earlier categories satisfy all of them. A condition may only name a stratification declared before it.

Stratifications group = [g1, g2] and subtype = [s1, s2] (only where group = g2)

A -> A_g1, A_g2_s1, A_g2_s2      3 compartments per bin instead of 4

conditional = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Conditional")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_stratification(
        id="subtype",
        categories=["s1", "s2"],
        conditions=[{"stratification": "group", "category": "g2"}],
    )
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=10000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.9},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.1},
        ],
        stratification_fractions=[
            {
                "stratification": "group",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "g1", "fraction": 0.6},
                    {"category": "g2", "fraction": 0.4},
                ],
            },
            {
                "stratification": "subtype",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "s1", "fraction": 0.5},
                    {"category": "s2", "fraction": 0.5},
                ],
            },
        ],
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

print([c.name for c in conditional.structure.initial_state()])
# ['A_g1', 'A_g2_s1', 'A_g2_s2', 'B_g1', 'B_g2_s1', 'B_g2_s2']

The fractions of a conditional stratification are fractions of the subgroup it splits, not of the total. subgroup_total multiplies along the chain to give the total of a subgroup, and get_conditioning_categories names the subgroup:

print(conditional.structure.subgroup_total())                # 10000
print(conditional.structure.subgroup_total(["g2"]))          # 10000 x 0.4 = 4000
print(conditional.structure.subgroup_total(["g2", "s1"]))    # 4000 x 0.5 = 2000
print(conditional.structure.get_conditioning_categories("subtype"))  # ('g2',)

See Conditional Stratifications for the full API.

docs.title: Per-compartment overrides
docs.text:
When the product of fractions cannot express the starting state, for example a state that is empty in only one category, compartment_fractions overrides single expanded compartments. Each fraction is a fraction of the total and replaces the product for that compartment only:

overridden = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Override")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=10000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.9},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.1},
        ],
        stratification_fractions=[
            {
                "stratification": "group",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "g1", "fraction": 0.5},
                    {"category": "g2", "fraction": 0.5},
                ],
            }
        ],
        compartment_fractions=[{"compartment": "B_g1", "fraction": 0.0}],
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

print({c.name: c.amount for c in overridden.structure.initial_state()})
# B_g1 starts empty; the other compartments keep their product
Rule Checked when Each name appears once, and each fraction is between 0.0 and 1.0 The conditions are set Each name is an expanded compartment The model is built The initial amounts do not sum to more than total The model is built

model.structure.update_compartment_fractions({"B_g1": 0.05}) changes or adds overrides on a built model.

docs.title: Updating fractions after building
docs.text:
overridden.structure.update_initial_conditions({"A": 0.85, "B": 0.15})
overridden.structure.update_stratification_fractions({"g1": 0.7})  # g2 becomes 0.3
Method Rule update_initial_conditions After the update, the bin fractions sum to 1.0. Move an amount between bins in one call. update_stratification_fractions Within each stratification you may omit one category; it receives what remains of 1.0. Omitting two raises.

A category name that two stratifications declare must be qualified with its stratification, as in {"group:g1": 0.5}. Calibration writes its results back through these same methods.

docs.title: Several sources or targets
docs.text:
A transition with several sources or targets moves one flow, like a reaction: each source loses it and each target gains it. Its rate must be absolute, because a per-capita rate has no single source to multiply.

reaction = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Reaction")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k", value=0.001)
    .add_transition(id="reaction", source=["A", "B"], target=["C", "C"], rate="k * A * B")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.5},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.5},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ],
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)
# Each step: A loses k*A*B, B loses k*A*B, C gains 2*k*A*B

For independent flows from several compartments, use the $compartment placeholder: the builder creates one transition per source. An empty target removes the flow from the system.

outflow = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Outflow")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_parameter(id="mu", value=0.01)
    .add_transition(id="outflow", source=["A", "B"], target=[], rate="mu * $compartment")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.5},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.5},
        ],
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)
print([t.id for t in outflow.structure.transitions])  # ['outflow__A', 'outflow__B']

docs.title: Steps and physical time
docs.text:
A model knows only steps: a rate is per step and a period is a number of steps. TimeScale gives a step a duration, and converts physical quantities to the step counts and per-step rates a model needs:

from commol import TimeScale

scale = TimeScale(step_seconds=60 * 60)  # one hour per step

print(scale.steps_per_day)        # 24
print(scale.steps_per_week)       # 168
print(scale.steps_from_days(3))   # 72

A period that is not a whole number of steps raises instead of rounding, so a step size that cannot express a period fails early:

daily = TimeScale(step_seconds=24 * 60 * 60)
try:
    daily.steps_from_hours(1)
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)
Method Returns rate_from_mean_duration(seconds) 1 - exp(-step / duration): the per-step rate for a mean time in a state rate_from_probability(p, period_steps) 1 - (1 - p) ** (1 / period_steps): applied over the period, it gives back p 
from commol import window_end, window_index, window_start

print(scale.rate_from_mean_duration(4 * 24 * 60 * 60))  # mean of 4 days
print(scale.rate_from_probability(0.3, scale.steps_per_week))

week = scale.steps_per_week
print(window_start(0, week), window_end(0, week))  # 0 168
print(window_index(168, week))                     # 0

The window grid (window_start, window_end, window_index) is in py-commol/commol/api/windows.py; see Windowed totals.

Rates for difference models only

rate_from_mean_duration and rate_from_probability return per-step probabilities, which a DifferenceEquations model applies once per step. A DifferentialEquations model integrates its rates in continuous time, so it needs the continuous rate: 1 / duration for a mean duration and -ln(1 - p) / period for a probability p over a period, both in steps. With the per-step value, the model moves too little.

A window covers the positions (start, end], the same interval that windowed observations use.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Three-State Model
docs.text:
A simple model with three states and two transitions:

from commol import ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Three-State Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="flow_AB", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ]
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example 2: Four-State Model with Intermediate States
docs.text:
Adding an intermediate state between A and B:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Four-State Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="M", name="Intermediate")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.4, description="A to M rate")
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.2, description="M to B rate")
    .add_parameter(id="k3", value=0.1, description="B to C rate")
    .add_transition(id="flow_AM", source=["A"], target=["M"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="flow_MB", source=["M"], target=["B"], rate="k2")
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k3")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.999},
            {"bin": "M", "fraction": 0.0},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.001},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ]
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example 3: Periodic (Time-Dependent) Rates
docs.text:
Modelling periodic variation in a transition rate:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Periodic Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k_mean", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k_amp", value=0.2)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(
        id="periodic_flow",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k_mean * (1 + k_amp * sin(2 * pi * step / 365)) * A * B / total"
    )
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ]
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=365 * 3)

docs.title: Example 4: Stratified Model with Group-Specific Rates
docs.text:
Different rates per category group:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Stratified Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2", "g3"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.0003)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_g1", value=0.15)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_g2", value=0.12)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_g3", value=0.08)
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1"
    )
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        stratified_rates=[
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "group", "category": "g1"}],
                "rate": "k2_g1"
            },
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "group", "category": "g2"}],
                "rate": "k2_g2"
            },
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "group", "category": "g3"}],
                "rate": "k2_g3"
            },
        ]
    )
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=10000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ],
        stratification_fractions=[
            {
                "stratification": "group",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "g1", "fraction": 0.25},
                    {"category": "g2", "fraction": 0.55},
                    {"category": "g3", "fraction": 0.20},
                ]
            }
        ]
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

print(f"B_g1: {results['B_g1'][-1]:.2f}")
print(f"B_g2: {results['B_g2'][-1]:.2f}")
print(f"B_g3: {results['B_g3'][-1]:.2f}")

docs.title: Example 5: Waning Effect (Cyclic Transition)
docs.text:
Entities in the final state gradually return to the initial state:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Cyclic Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_parameter(id="k3", value=0.01)  # Return rate
    .add_transition(id="flow_AB", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .add_transition(id="return_CA", source=["C"], target=["A"], rate="k3")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ]
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=1000)

docs.title: Example 6: Capacity-Constrained Rate
docs.text:
The flow rate slows as a downstream compartment approaches a capacity limit:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Capacity Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.5)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_max", value=0.15)
    .add_parameter(id="capacity", value=100.0)
    .add_transition(id="flow_AB", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        rate="k2_max * (1 - max(0, (B - capacity) / capacity))"
    )
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.95},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.05},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ]
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example 7: Multi-Stratified Model with Intersection Rates
docs.text:
A model with two stratifications and a rate specific to a particular intersection of categories:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Multi-Stratified Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_stratification(id="type", categories=["t1", "t2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1_low", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k1_high", value=0.6)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1_low * A * B / total",
        stratified_rates=[
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "type", "category": "t2"}],
                "rate": "k1_high * A * B / total"
            }
        ]
    )
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ],
        stratification_fractions=[
            {
                "stratification": "group",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "g1", "fraction": 0.6},
                    {"category": "g2", "fraction": 0.4},
                ]
            },
            {
                "stratification": "type",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "t1", "fraction": 0.8},
                    {"category": "t2", "fraction": 0.2},
                ]
            }
        ]
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example 8: Subgroup-Normalized Rate
docs.text:
The engine computes the subgroup total total_<category>. This example divides a rate by the total of its subgroup instead of the total of the model:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Subgroup-Normalized Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.4)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1 * A * B / total",
        stratified_rates=[
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "group", "category": "g1"}],
                "rate": "k1 * A * B / total_g1"  # Divided by the subgroup total
            }
        ]
    )
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ],
        stratification_fractions=[
            {
                "stratification": "group",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "g1", "fraction": 0.5},
                    {"category": "g2", "fraction": 0.5},
                ]
            }
        ]
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example 9: Conditional Stratification
docs.text:
A second stratification that only applies to a subset of the first. Here, the subtype stratification only expands g2 compartments — g1 compartments are not split further.

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Conditional Stratification Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    # group applies to all compartments
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    # subtype only applies to g2 compartments
    .add_stratification(
        id="subtype",
        categories=["s1", "s2"],
        conditions=[{"stratification": "group", "category": "g2"}]
    )
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_default", value=0.1)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_s1", value=0.15)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_s2", value=0.05)
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1 * A * B / total"
    )
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        rate="k2_default",
        stratified_rates=[
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "subtype", "category": "s1"}],
                "rate": "k2_s1"
            },
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "subtype", "category": "s2"}],
                "rate": "k2_s2"
            },
        ]
    )
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=10000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ],
        stratification_fractions=[
            {
                "stratification": "group",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "g1", "fraction": 0.6},
                    {"category": "g2", "fraction": 0.4},
                ]
            },
            {
                "stratification": "subtype",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "s1", "fraction": 0.7},
                    {"category": "s2", "fraction": 0.3},
                ]
            }
        ]
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

# Generated compartments:
# A_g1, B_g1, C_g1          (group=g1, no subtype)
# A_g2_s1, B_g2_s1, C_g2_s1 (group=g2, subtype=s1)
# A_g2_s2, B_g2_s2, C_g2_s2 (group=g2, subtype=s2)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

print(f"B_g1:    {results['B_g1'][-1]:.2f}")
print(f"B_g2_s1: {results['B_g2_s1'][-1]:.2f}")
print(f"B_g2_s2: {results['B_g2_s2'][-1]:.2f}")

docs.title: Example 10: Parameter Calibration
docs.text:
Calibrate model parameters to match observed data:

from commol import (
    ModelBuilder,
    Simulation,
    Calibrator,
    CalibrationProblem,
    CalibrationParameter,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    ParticleSwarmConfig,
)

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Model for Calibration", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=None)   # To be calibrated
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=None)   # To be calibrated
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1 * A * B / total"
    )
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        rate="k2 * B"
    )
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
            {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
        ]
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=0,  output="B", value=10.0),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=10, output="B", value=45.2),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=20, output="B", value=78.5),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=30, output="B", value=62.3),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=40, output="B", value=38.1),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=50, output="B", value=18.7),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=60, output="B", value=8.2),
]

simulation = Simulation(model)

parameters = [
    CalibrationParameter(
        id="k1",
        parameter_type="parameter",
        min_bound=0.0,
        max_bound=1.0,
        initial_guess=0.3
    ),
    CalibrationParameter(
        id="k2",
        parameter_type="parameter",
        min_bound=0.0,
        max_bound=1.0,
        initial_guess=0.1
    ),
]

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=parameters,
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=ParticleSwarmConfig(
        num_particles=30,
        max_iterations=500,
        verbose=True
    ),
)

calibrator = Calibrator(simulation, problem)
result = calibrator.run()

print(f"Converged: {result.converged}")
print(f"Iterations: {result.iterations}")
print(f"Final loss: {result.final_loss:.6f}")
print(f"k1: {result.best_parameters['k1']:.6f}")
print(f"k2: {result.best_parameters['k2']:.6f}")

model.update_parameters(result.best_parameters)
calibrated_sim = Simulation(model)
results = calibrated_sim.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example: Time-Pattern Driven Transition
docs.text:
A composed time-varying transition: an opening pulse, a monthly periodic event, and a continuous seasonal baseline.

from commol import ModelBuilder, Simulation, AxisPattern

rate = AxisPattern.combine(
    AxisPattern.pulse(at=0, value=0.3),
    AxisPattern.periodic(period=30, value=0.05),
    AxisPattern.seasonal(amplitude=0.005, period=365, baseline=0.01),
)

model = (
    ModelBuilder("AB-time-varying")
    .add_bin("A", "Source")
    .add_bin("B", "Sink")
    .add_transition("flow", ["A"], ["B"], rate=rate)
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=10_000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 1.0},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.0},
        ],
    )
    .build("DifferenceEquations")
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=365)

docs.title: Example: Sub-Group Specific Schedules
docs.text:
Different stratification sub-groups receive different patterns. The schedule is built by chaining AxisPattern.add_group(...) calls — the first call on the class itself, subsequent calls on the returned instance:

from commol import ModelBuilder, Simulation, AxisPattern

rate = (
    AxisPattern.add_group(
        conditions=[{"stratification": "group", "category": "cat1"}],
        schedule=AxisPattern.periodic(period=7, value=0.05),
    )
    .add_group(
        conditions=[{"stratification": "group", "category": "cat2"}],
        schedule=AxisPattern.periodic(period=30, value=0.05),
    )
)

model = (
    ModelBuilder("AB-stratified-schedule")
    .add_bin("A", "Source")
    .add_bin("B", "Sink")
    .add_stratification("group", ["cat1", "cat2"])
    .add_transition("flow", ["A"], ["B"], rate=rate)
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[
            {"bin": "A", "fraction": 1.0},
            {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.0},
        ],
        stratification_fractions=[
            {
                "stratification": "group",
                "fractions": [
                    {"category": "cat1", "fraction": 0.5},
                    {"category": "cat2", "fraction": 0.5},
                ],
            }
        ],
    )
    .build("DifferenceEquations")
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=60)

docs.title: Mathematical Expressions
docs.text:
Back to Home

Rates and formula parameters are written as expressions, such as "k1 * A * B / total". This page lists everything an expression can contain: operators, variables, functions, and the security limits. The engine compiles each expression to machine code (Cranelift) once, and reuses it at every step.

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
from commol import ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Expressions")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k1_seasonal", value="k1 * (1 + 0.3 * sin(2 * pi * step / 365))")
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1_seasonal * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_ba", source=["B"], target=["A"], rate="if(step > 30, 0.05, 0)")
    .set_initial_conditions(
        total=1000,
        bin_fractions=[{"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99}, {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01}],
    )
    .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=60)
Where Example Evaluated Transition rate "k1 * A * B / total" For every flow, at every step Formula parameter value "k1 * 2" At every step, in declaration order, before the rates Stratified rate rate "k_g1 * A" Like a transition rate Calibration constraint expression "k1 - k2" See Model Calibration

Whether a rate is the flow itself or a rate per member of the source depends on the variables it names; see Absolute and per-capita rates.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
Operator Meaning Example Value +, - Addition, subtraction, negation "k1 - k2", "-k1" *, / Multiplication, division "k1 * B / total" % Remainder "step % 7" 0 to 6 ** or ^ Power "2 * 3 ** 4" 162 ( ) Grouping "(2 + 3) * 4" 20 >, <, >=, <=, ==, != Comparison, only inside if "if(step > 30, k1, 0)" ! Not, only inside if "if(!(step > 30), k1, 0)"

Precedence, from high to low: parentheses, power, multiplication, division and remainder, addition and subtraction. So "2 ** 3 * 4" is 32 and "2 + 3 * 4" is 14.

A comparison gives a boolean, not a number, so it cannot be multiplied: "k1 * (step > 30)" is rejected. Write "if(step > 30, k1, 0)". Rates do not accept && or ||; nest if calls instead:

in_window = "if(step >= 10, if(step <= 20, 0.05, 0), 0)"   # 0.05 for steps 10 to 20
outside = "if(step < 10, 0.05, if(step > 20, 0.05, 0))"    # 0.05 outside that window

docs.title: Variables
docs.text: Variable Value A parameter id The parameter's value at this step A bin id, without stratifications The bin's amount A compartment name, such as A_g1 That compartment's amount A bin id, with stratifications The total of all its compartments total The total: the sum of every compartment, accumulators excluded t The current position on the axis. A difference model reads it at each step, so there it equals step; a differential model reads it anywhere step The step that holds the current position, floor(t): 0, 1, 2, … It is constant on each unit interval of a differential model; see Time inside a step pi, e π and e

docs.title: Subgroup totals
docs.text:
With stratifications, the engine also provides sums of compartments, the subgroup totals. Category suffixes must follow the order in which the stratifications were declared. commol_rs.model.subgroup_total_names (in crates/commol-model/src/builder.rs) lists them for a structure.

Variable Sum of Example (group then type) total_<cat>… Every compartment with these categories total_g1, total_t1, total_g1_t1 <bin> Every compartment of the bin A <bin>_<cat>… The bin's compartments with these categories A_g1, A_t1; with every category, the compartment itself (A_g1_t1) 
from commol import ModelBuilder

def value_of(expression: str) -> float:
    """The value of an expression at step 0, read through a formula parameter."""
    model = (
        ModelBuilder(name="Variables")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
        .add_stratification(id="type", categories=["t1", "t2"])
        .add_parameter(id="probe", value=expression)
        .add_transition(id="probe_flow", source=[], target=["B"], rate="probe")
        .set_initial_conditions(
            total=1000,
            bin_fractions=[{"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.6}, {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.4}],
            stratification_fractions=[
                {
                    "stratification": "group",
                    "fractions": [
                        {"category": "g1", "fraction": 0.25},
                        {"category": "g2", "fraction": 0.75},
                    ],
                },
                {
                    "stratification": "type",
                    "fractions": [
                        {"category": "t1", "fraction": 0.5},
                        {"category": "t2", "fraction": 0.5},
                    ],
                },
            ],
        )
        .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
    )
    results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=1)
    inflow = sum(series[1] - series[0] for series in results.values())
    return inflow / 4  # the probe flows into each of the 4 B compartments

print(value_of("total + 0"))        # 1000.0
print(value_of("total_g1 + 0"))     # 250.0  = 1000 x 0.25
print(value_of("total_g1_t1 + 0"))  # 125.0  = 1000 x 0.25 x 0.5
print(value_of("A + 0"))        # 600.0
print(value_of("A_g1 + 0"))     # 150.0  = 600 x 0.25
print(value_of("A_t1 + 0"))     # 300.0  = 600 x 0.5
Pitfall Result Suffixes out of declaration order, as in A_t1_g1 Error: the variable is not found total_… out of order, as in total_t1_g1 build fails and lists the valid total_… names A combination that a conditional stratification never creates build fails for total_…; <bin>_… is not found

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Group Functions Trigonometric sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2(y, x) Hyperbolic sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh Exponential and logarithm exp, log (natural), ln (natural), log10, log2 Power and root sqrt, cbrt, pow(x, y), hypot(x, y) Comparison min(a, b), max(a, b), abs Rounding floor, ceil, round (halves round up: round(2.5) is 3) Conditional if(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)

For rates that change over time, AxisPattern builds tested expressions for pulses, windows, ramps and seasons.

docs.title: Common patterns
docs.text:
patterns = {
    "mass action": "k1 * A * B",
    "frequency dependent": "k1 * A * B / total",
    "saturation": "k1 * B / (1 + B)",
    "linear growth over time": "0.1 + 0.001 * step",
    "exponential decay over time": "k1 * exp(-0.01 * step)",
    "annual cycle": "k1 * (1 + 0.3 * sin(2 * pi * step / 365))",
    "never negative": "max(0, k1 - 0.001 * step)",
    "capped above a threshold": "k1 * min(1, 100 / max(B, 1))",
    "only after step 30": "if(step > 30, k1, 0)",
    "safe division": "k1 * B / max(total, 1)",
}

To keep a rate readable, move part of it into a formula parameter: add_parameter(id="k1_seasonal", value="k1 * (1 + 0.3 * sin(2 * pi * step / 365))") and then rate="k1_seasonal * A * B / total".

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Every rate and constraint expression is checked before it reaches the engine (commol.utils.security.validate_expression_security). An expression that is not plain mathematics is rejected when the transition is added:

try:
    ModelBuilder(name="Unsafe").add_bin(id="A", name="State A").add_transition(
        id="t", source=["A"], target=[], rate="__import__('os')"
    )
except ValueError as error:
    print("rejected")
Limit (SecurityConfig) Value Expression length 10000 characters Nesting depth 10 levels Function calls 500 Variable name length 50 characters Numeric literal 1e12 Complexity score 1000

docs.title: Probabilistic Calibration
docs.text:
Back to Model Calibration

A single calibration gives one parameter set. A probabilistic calibration gives an ensemble: many parameter sets that all fit the data, and from them, prediction intervals and parameter spreads. Add a probabilistic_config to the problem and call Calibrator.run_probabilistic().

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
import random

from commol import (
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    ParticleSwarmConfig,
    ProbabilisticCalibrationConfig,
    ProbNsga2Config,
    Simulation,
)

def model(k1: float | None, k2: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Ensemble")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .set_initial_conditions(
            total=1000,
            bin_fractions=[
                {"bin": "A", "fraction": 0.99},
                {"bin": "B", "fraction": 0.01},
                {"bin": "C", "fraction": 0.0},
            ],
        )
        .build(engine="DifferenceEquations")
    )

# Noisy observations of a model with k1 = 0.4, k2 = 0.1
truth = Simulation(model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=50)
noise = random.Random(1)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step] * (1 + noise.gauss(0, 0.05)))
    for step in range(5, 51, 5)
]

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.01, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    optimization_config=ParticleSwarmConfig(num_particles=20, max_iterations=100),
    probabilistic_config=ProbabilisticCalibrationConfig(
        n_runs=8,
        ensemble_selection=ProbNsga2Config(
            ensemble_size_mode="bounded",
            ensemble_size_min=5,
            ensemble_size_max=10,
            population_size=40,
            generations=30,
        ),
    ),
    seed=11,
)

result = Calibrator(Simulation(model(None, None)), problem).run_probabilistic()
ensemble = result.selected_ensemble

print(ensemble.ensemble_size)                            # 10
print({k: round(v, 2) for k, v in sorted(ensemble.point_parameters.items())})
# {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}
print(ensemble.coverage_percentage)                      # 100.0: every observation inside the band
k1 = ensemble.parameter_statistics["k1"]
print(round(k1.percentile_lower, 2), round(k1.percentile_upper, 2))  # the 95% interval of k1

The settings above are small so the example is fast. For real work, see A recommended configuration.

docs.title: How the ensemble is built
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[n_runs calibrations] --> B[Filter and deduplicate evaluations]
    B --> C[Cluster candidates]
    C --> D[Pick diverse representatives]
    D --> E[Select the ensemble]
    E --> F[Intervals per member]
  1. Runs. The optimizer runs n_runs times, from different random starts, and every evaluation it makes is kept.
  2. Filter. Duplicate parameter sets are removed, and only near-optimal ones are kept (evaluation_processing).
  3. Cluster. Candidates are grouped in parameter space or in the space of the predictions that are compared with data (clustering).
  4. Representatives. Diverse candidates are taken from each cluster (representative_selection).
  5. Selection. NSGA-II (default) or a fit-gated greedy search picks the final members, balancing narrow intervals and coverage of the observations (ensemble_selection).
  6. Intervals. Each member's predictions are computed with the observation's aggregates, windows and scale factors, and then reduced across members.

Every loss works ("sse", "rmse", "mae"): the ensemble is scored with the same loss as the runs. Use normalize_observations=True when series differ in size.

docs.title: ProbabilisticCalibrationConfig
docs.text: Field Default Meaning n_runs 10 Independent calibrations. evaluation_processing ProbEvaluationFilterConfig() Which evaluations become candidates. clustering ProbClusteringConfig() How candidates are grouped. representative_selection ProbRepresentativeConfig() How many candidates reach the selection, and which. ensemble_selection ProbNsga2Config() The selection backend: ProbNsga2Config or ProbGreedyLocalSearchConfig. confidence_level 0.95 The level of every interval. include_ensemble_candidates False Adds the candidates and their losses to the result.

docs.title: ProbEvaluationFilterConfig
docs.text: Field Default Meaning evaluation_retention "all" "all", "best_per_run" or "top_k_per_run" evaluations of each run. top_k_per_run None How many, with "top_k_per_run". max_loss_ratio None Keeps only evaluations whose loss is at most this times the best one: the core pool. tail_max_loss_ratio, tail_max_representatives None, 0 A wider loss band from which up to that many candidates are added, only if their predictions are new. loss_percentile_filter 1.0 Keeps this best fraction, by loss. deduplication_tolerance 1e-6 Parameter sets closer than this are duplicates. min_evaluations_required 5 The minimum number of unique evaluations the analysis needs.

docs.title: ProbClusteringConfig
docs.text: Field Default Meaning feature_space "parameters" "parameters", or "observed_predictions" to cluster what is compared with data (windows, aggregates and scale factors included). n_clusters None None chooses it by silhouette score, up to max_k (10). min_evaluations_for_clustering 100 Below it, no clustering. silhouette_threshold, silhouette_excellent_threshold 0.2, 0.8 When clustering helps, and when to stop searching. kmeans_algorithm, kmeans_max_iter "elkan", 100 K-means settings. silhouette_sample_size, minibatch_kmeans_threshold None Speed settings for many evaluations. identical_solutions_atol 1e-10 Tolerance for identical solutions.

docs.title: ProbRepresentativeConfig
docs.text: Field Default Meaning max_representatives 1000 Candidates passed to the selection. percentage_elite_cluster_selection 0.1 Share of each cluster's best solutions always included. cluster_representative_strategy "proportional" "proportional" or "equal" representatives per cluster. cluster_selection_method "latin_hypercube" "latin_hypercube", "crowding_distance" or "maximin_distance". quality_temperature, sparsity_weight 1.0, 2.0 "maximin_distance" weighting. k_neighbors_min, k_neighbors_max 5, 10 Density estimate. stratum_fit_weight 10.0 "latin_hypercube" weighting.

docs.title: Ensemble selection
docs.text:
Both backends share the size settings:

Field Default Meaning ensemble_size_mode "automatic" "fixed", "bounded" or "automatic". ensemble_size None The size, with "fixed". ensemble_size_min, ensemble_size_max None The range, with "bounded". ProbNsga2Config field Default Meaning population_size, generations 100, 100 NSGA-II effort. crossover_probability 0.9 NSGA-II crossover. pareto_preference 0.5 Which Pareto solution is reported: towards narrow intervals or towards coverage. ProbGreedyLocalSearchConfig field Default Meaning central_fit_max_loss_ratio 1.25 Rejects an ensemble whose median prediction loses more than this times the best member. search_beam_width 32 Partial ensembles kept per size; more is wider and slower.

docs.title: A recommended configuration
docs.text:
from commol import (
    ProbClusteringConfig,
    ProbEvaluationFilterConfig,
    ProbGreedyLocalSearchConfig,
    ProbRepresentativeConfig,
)

recommended = ProbabilisticCalibrationConfig(
    n_runs=75,
    evaluation_processing=ProbEvaluationFilterConfig(
        evaluation_retention="top_k_per_run",
        top_k_per_run=100,
        max_loss_ratio=1.25,
        tail_max_loss_ratio=2.0,
        tail_max_representatives=50,
    ),
    clustering=ProbClusteringConfig(feature_space="observed_predictions"),
    representative_selection=ProbRepresentativeConfig(
        max_representatives=1000,
        percentage_elite_cluster_selection=0.5,
        cluster_selection_method="maximin_distance",
    ),
    ensemble_selection=ProbNsga2Config(
        ensemble_size_mode="bounded",
        ensemble_size_min=15,
        ensemble_size_max=30,
        population_size=100,
        generations=100,
        pareto_preference=0.5,
    ),
)

# The fit-gated alternative to NSGA-II
greedy = ProbGreedyLocalSearchConfig(
    ensemble_size_mode="bounded",
    ensemble_size_min=15,
    ensemble_size_max=30,
    central_fit_max_loss_ratio=1.25,
    search_beam_width=32,
)

Raise n_runs, particles and iterations before you relax the loss gates. If the intervals are narrow because every near-optimal candidate predicts the same, prefer a small prediction-novel tail (tail_max_*) over a larger max_loss_ratio: a wider band only helps when its members still fit the data.

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
ProbabilisticCalibrationResult field Meaning selected_ensemble The EnsembleSolution below. selection_algorithm "nsga2" or "greedy_local_search". pareto_front, selected_pareto_index NSGA-II only: the Pareto summaries (EnsembleSelectionSummary) and the reported one. n_runs_performed, n_unique_evaluations, n_clusters_used What the pipeline did. confidence_level The interval level. stage_timings, stage_counts Seconds and counts per stage. ensemble_candidates With include_ensemble_candidates=True. EnsembleSolution field Meaning point_parameters, point_loss The lowest-loss member: the only parameter set that describes one calibrated model. ensemble_parameters, ensemble_size Every member. parameter_statistics Per parameter: mean, median, std, percentile_lower, percentile_upper, min, max. prediction_positions The positions of the prediction series: the unit grid up to one past the last observation, and every observation position and window start. prediction_median, prediction_ci_lower, prediction_ci_upper Per output, one value per position of prediction_positions. windowed_prediction_* The same for windowed observations, at the positions in windowed_prediction_positions. coverage_percentage, average_ci_width Share of observations inside the band, and the band's mean width. central_loss The loss of the member-wise median prediction. observation_diagnostics Coverage and width per observed series. selection_diagnostics Why the selection stopped where it did. 
print(ensemble.observation_diagnostics["B"]["coverage_percentage"])  # 100.0

Use point_parameters to build a model

apply_calibration_parameters applies point_parameters. Do not combine the parameter medians into a model: that parameter set may never have been calibrated and need not fit the data.

Check observation_diagnostics for every series: a good overall coverage can hide a poor fit of a small series.

docs.title: Your own ensemble statistics
docs.text:
Simulate each member, reduce each run to the quantity you need, then take statistics across members with member_statistics:

from commol import ci_percentiles, member_statistics

final_c = [
    Simulation(model(member["k1"], member["k2"])).run(num_steps=50)["C"][-1]
    for member in ensemble.ensemble_parameters
]
stats = member_statistics(final_c, result.confidence_level)
print(sorted(stats))  # ['ci_lower', 'ci_upper', 'max', 'mean', 'median', 'min']

print(ci_percentiles(0.95))  # the percentile points of a 95% interval: about (2.5, 97.5)

member_statistics also accepts equal-length series and reduces them position by position.

Reduce each member first

Bands of raw trajectories, reduced afterwards, give a difference of percentiles: an interval that no member realizes, and usually a wider one. windowed_prediction_* already follow this rule.
